Better to beg forgiveness (permalink)

From its inception, I've loved Creative Commons. I hung out with Lisa Rein, Matt Haughey and Aaron Swartz while they coded up the first version of the site, and my first novel, Down and Out in the Magic Kingdom, was the first professionally published text ever released under a CC license, just weeks after CC itself launched:

https://creativecommons.org/

In those early days, CC licenses were primarily of interest to people who were steeped in copyright law, lore and litigation; so many of the early debates about these licenses turned on esoteric (but important!) questions about copyright; for example, how CC would interact with copyright's "limitations and exceptions."

You see, copyright has never meant the absolute right to control all uses of a work. Every system of copyright includes a set of "limitations and exceptions" for people making use of copyrighted works without permission, even if the copyright holder objects to that use. The best-known example of this is "fair use," a concept from American law.

Fair use is (potentially) extremely broad, but it's also extremely "fact-intensive" – that's the phrase lawyers use to describe the kind of legal question whose answer is almost always "it depends." Fair use might let you copy the entirety of a work, even for a commercial purpose. It might let you create new works based on existing works. It might let you do these things specifically to discourage people from buying the original. But…it depends.

If you know anything about fair use, it's probably something about a "four-step test" used to determine if a usage is fair. These four steps are just questions a judge might ask of someone who's been sued for copyright infringement, but who claims that they were making a fair use. The questions are:

I. What was the "nature and purpose" of your use? Were you doing something "transformative?" Were you criticizing the work? Were you using the work for educational purposes?

II. What was the nature of the work you used? Was it primarily factual (like a news article) or creative (like a short story)?

III. How much of the work did you take? Did you take more than you needed to transform the work, to accomplish your criticism, to teach someone?

IV. What impact did your use have on the original? Did the copyright holder lose money as a result of your use?

https://fairuse.stanford.edu/overview/fair-use/four-factors/

These questions are indeed enshrined in US copyright law, but (for better and for worse) you can't figure out if a use is "fair" just by asking these questions. Fair use is ultimately subject to "the rule of reason," a legal principle meaning that the law shouldn't result in obviously stupid restrictions. What's "obviously stupid?" Well, that's the tricky part – you'll have to convince a judge!

For example, the author of a book called The Wind Done Gone was sued for taking the characters, plot and setting of Gone With the Wind in order to tell the same story from the perspective of the enslaved Africans who were denied agency and moral consideration in the original. The court found for The Wind Done Gone:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Done_Gone

Wind Done Gone took the "heart" of Gone With the Wind (III), but then again, Done Gone was highly transformative (I), Gone With was also a work of fiction, entitled to the highest level of protection (II). Even worse, the point of Done Gone was to point out the gross defects in Gone With (I) and thus directly undermine sales and licensing for the original (IV). Anyone who claims you can answer fair use controversies by running through the four factors as though they were a checklist really doesn't understand fair use:

https://pluralistic.net/2022/02/06/crypto-copyright-%f0%9f%a4%a1%f0%9f%92%a9/

But even after you've acquired an appreciation of the fact-intensive, nuanced flexibility of fair use, you still don't understand copyright's limitations and exceptions. Fair use is important, but there's also "first sale," the doctrine that says that after you buy something, you own it, and copyright can't be used to interfere with your traditional property rights. That's why you can buy and sell used books, paintings, records, and other copyrighted work, even if they are sold with fine print that says you're not allowed to:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirtsaeng_v._John_Wiley_%26_Sons,_Inc.

When it comes to copyright's limitations and exceptions, "fair use" and "first sale" are the big ones, but just as important are the small ones – the really small ones. Like other laws, copyright is subject to the principle of "di minimis" (from a longer Latin phrase that translates as "the law does not concern itself with trifles"):

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_minimis

Technically, it may be trespassing to step on someone else's yard. But if your shoe brushes up against their lawn while you're walking on the sidewalk out front of their house, it's not trespassing. Or if it is trespassing, it's a di minimis trespass, too small to matter to the law. A lot of potential copyright violations – like taking a picture of a passage in a book and posting it to social media – are so small that we don't need to apply a fair use analysis to them. They're trifles, and "the law does not concern itself with trifles."

These limitations and exceptions all apply without permission from rightsholders. They apply even if they make rightsholders furious. They are your rights, as a member of the public, as a purchaser of a work, or just as someone who whistles a song that's stuck in your head.

And that's where the esoteric early Creative Commons copyright debate comes in. Creative Commons is a way to formally codify and convey permission to use copyrighted works. Without Creative Commons, it's really hard – and expensive – to provide legally reliable permission to someone else to use something you've created.

If I want to let you adapt one of my short stories for the stage, we should both probably hire copyright lawyers at several hundred dollars per hour to draft and review a contract setting out what my permission really means. Worse: even after we've paid the lawyers, neither of us will likely really understand the fine legal technicalities of the deal. We just have to take the lawyers' word for it that the complex jargon in the contract is sufficient for our purposes. Between the complexity and the expense, there are lots of potential creative collaborations that would cost so much to paper over that they're just not worth doing, even if they'd delight everyone involved.

Creative Commons cuts through this with its standardized licenses, which spell out in plain language which permissions are being granted. Even better, these licenses are international, translated into the language and laws of dozens of countries. That means that you can take a CC licensed short story from Japan, animate it using CC licensed 3D models from Italy, set it to a CC licensed soundtrack from Indonesia and release it in Ukraine, and the whole thing just works.

Those uses – turning a story into an animation, using a 3D model, syncing a soundtrack to a video – are all pretty ambitious uses, especially if you're going to make the final result indefinitely available to the general public. It makes sense to paper over these uses, and Creative Commons makes that legal work as simple as linking to your sources and their licenses in your final product.

But there are plenty of uses that don't need licenses – even ambitious ones. Remember Wind Done Gone? There are circumstances when you can adapt someone else's story without permission, relying instead on a limitation or exception to copyright. And of course, there are plenty of trivial uses – pasting a photo into your groupchat, say – that are di minimis and also don't need permission.

These copyright flexibilities are critical. Imagine if you could only criticize someone's work if they gave you permission to do so! From the founding of CC, copyfighters raised serious concerns that CC would teach people that they can only remix other people's work if they have a license, be it a CC license or the kind that you negotiate with a lawyer.

Today – 25 years later!- CC is an unqualified success. Without CC, we wouldn't have Wikipedia! You find CC licenses on Youtube, Flickr, Bandcamp, the Internet Archive, and in many of the most important scholarly and scientific journals in the world.

But, also, 25 years later, the world is even more convinced that you should always ask permission: "better safe than sorry." I don't know if CC contributed to this culture of timidity. More likely, it was bullying copyright trolls who terrorized people into a reflex of asking permission for everything, always.

As the creator of more than 30 books, hundreds of collages, and tens of thousands of essays and blog-posts, I am often on the receiving end of these permission requests.

For example, people often ask me if they can use my CC licensed works in ways that the associated licenses clearly permit. I'm sure the people who email me for permission to do things I've already granted them permission to do think they're being polite, but I really wish they'd stop. When someone asks me if they can make a use permitted by my CC licenses, I need to carefully parse through their use to make sure they're not asking for something more.

This is time-consuming work that often involves several volleys of email just to confirm that, no, they're just asking if they can do something I've already told them they can do. This is not a good use of anyone's time! By all means, drop me a note with a link to something you've remixed from my work. That's fun! It's a lot more fun than making me play detective in order to figure out if you're exceeding the license's permissions.

There are also a lot of requests that clearly amount to fair use and/or di minimis usage. You don't need to email me to get my permission to read a brief passage from one of my books on your Youtube video! You don't need my permission to quote one of my stories in an English exam! What's more, the world would be a lot shittier if you did, so let's not act as though that's reasonable behavior, lest we shift the (already far too restrictive) norms, which might even lead to a legal change.

Finally, there's the people who email me about their desire to make uses that are more (ahem) ambitious, but that no one could possibly find out about or get angry over…except for the fact that they emailed me to ask my permission.

You want to make a tiny bootleg edition of one of my novels for your anarchist book fair? That's totally a copyright infringement, it's super-illegal, and if my publisher found out about it, I'm sure they'd send you a sphincter-puckering legal letter telling you to knock it off (and maybe even demanding that you disgorge the seven dollars, three bottlecaps and eleven cool feathers you took in trade for those pirate books).

But my publisher won't ever find out about it – unless you email me asking for permission. I absolutely cannot give you permission to do this. I have a contract with my publisher promising that I will never authorize someone other than them to publish that book. Once you tell me about your intention to do this, I'm obliged to tell my publisher, so that they can tell you no in language that would strip paint off a barn.

Buying a classroom set of books, but you also want to paste chunks of one of my books into your educational institution's classroom intranet for use as a teaching aid? There's no way my publisher would ever find out you did that, and if they did, sure, you'd also get a blood-curdling legal letter. But dude, all my books are DRM-free. You could have just pasted the text into your CMS. In what universe is my publisher going to pay one of their lawyers to review, adjudicate and paper over your request to make a use that you're not proposing to pay them for?

Let's be clear: I'm not giving you permission to pirate my work. I already spend far too much of my time chasing down dickheads who sell competing editions of my books on Amazon and Audible. I'm sick to the back teeth of wrangling Ingram's takedown process to get rid of bootleg print editions of my books.

What I'm saying is, all of your interactions with copyrighted works need not involve the author and publisher. There is a whole universe of uses that might technically violate copyright, might technically not fit into di minimis, first sale or fair use – but these are also uses that no one would ever find out.

I get it. You may feel like you can't tell the difference between the kind of uses that no one would give a shit about; the uses that might attract a bone-chilling lawyer letter; and the uses that might land you in court. I'm sorry, but I can't help you figure that one out. I'm not a lawyer. Even if I was, I'm not your lawyer.

This is one of those areas where I break with my friend, the wonderful John Hodgman. On his indispensable podcast "Judge John Hodgman," he frequently admonishes people who are uncertain if they're overstepping a bound in a commercial establishment to ask an employee for permission. For example: should you fill up a water glass with soda water from a self-serve dispenser?

https://maximumfun.org/podcasts/judge-john-hodgman/

John says you should always ask the cashier. But I've worked jobs like that, and I can tell you that there were plenty of jobs where my boss felt very strongly that taking $0.0000001 worth of water and bubbles without paying for it was theft…and where I thought my boss was a dick for thinking that. If I pretended I didn't see you getting a glass of fizzy water, the worst that would happen is my boss would tell me to keep a closer eye on the customers lest they steal his precious CO2. But if you asked me whether you could fill your glass, and my boss caught me saying yes, I'd be fired.

There's a lot of normal, perfectly fine stuff that technically violates copyright that I can't give you permission to do, because I've signed a contract with my publisher. If you ask me, I'll have to ask my editor, who will say no, even though he thinks it's fine, too. If I push it, he'll have to ask the lawyers, who will almost certainly also say no, even if they think it's fine, because it doesn't make sense to spend hours papering over a legal agreement with someone who wants to sell seven copies of a book at an anarchist book-fair or upload a couple chapters of a book to a school's intranet.

Are there instances in which you might misjudge which category your use falls under and end up in court? I guess so. But if that's your concern, asking my permission does no good, because I'm just gonna tell you no.

Life is hard.

Read books.

Like other laws, copyright is subject to the principle of "di minimis" (from a longer Latin phrase that translates as "the law does not concern itself with trifles"): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_minimis Technically, it may be trespassing to step on someone else's yard. But if your shoe brushes up against their lawn while you're walking on the sidewalk out front of their house, it's not trespassing. Or if it is trespassing, it's a di minimis trespass, too small to matter to the law. A lot of potential copyright violations – like taking a picture of a passage in a book and posting it to social media – are so small that we don't need to apply a fair use analysis to them. They're trifles, and "the law does not concern itself with trifles." These limitations and exceptions all apply without permission from rightsholders. They apply even if they make rightsholders furious. They are your rights, as a member of the public, as a purchaser of a work, or just as someone who whistles a song that's stuck in your head. And that's where the esoteric early Creative Commons copyright debate comes in. Creative Commons is a way to formally codify and convey permission to use copyrighted works. Without Creative Commons, it's really hard – and expensive – to provide legally reliable permission to someone else to use something you've created. If I want to let you adapt one of my short stories for the stage, we should both probably hire copyright lawyers at several hundred dollars per hour to draft and review a contract setting out what my permission really means. Worse: even after we've paid the lawyers, neither of us will likely really understand the fine legal technicalities of the deal. We just have to take the lawyers' word for it that the complex jargon in the contract is sufficient for our purposes. Between the complexity and the expense, there are lots of potential creative collaborations that would cost so much to paper over that they're just not worth doing, even if they'd delight everyone involved. Creative Commons cuts through this with its standardized licenses, which spell out in plain language which permissions are being granted. Even better, these licenses are international, translated into the language and laws of dozens of countries. That means that you can take a CC licensed short story from Japan, animate it using CC licensed 3D models from Italy, set it to a CC licensed soundtrack from Indonesia and release it in Ukraine, and the whole thing just works. Those uses – turning a story into an animation, using a 3D model, syncing a soundtrack to a video – are all pretty ambitious uses, especially if you're going to make the final result indefinitely available to the general public. It makes sense to paper over these uses, and Creative Commons makes that legal work as simple as linking to your sources and their licenses in your final product. But there are plenty of uses that don't need licenses – even ambitious ones. Remember Wind Done Gone? There are circumstances when you can adapt someone else's story without permission, relying instead on a limitation or exception to copyright. And of course, there are plenty of trivial uses – pasting a photo into your groupchat, say – that are di minimis and also don't need permission. These copyright flexibilities are critical. Imagine if you could only criticize someone's work if they gave you permission to do so! From the founding of CC, copyfighters raised serious concerns that CC would teach people that they can only remix other people's work if they have a license, be it a CC license or the kind that you negotiate with a lawyer. Today – 25 years later!- CC is an unqualified success. Without CC, we wouldn't have Wikipedia! You find CC licenses on Youtube, Flickr, Bandcamp, the Internet Archive, and in many of the most important scholarly and scientific journals in the world. But, also, 25 years later, the world is even more convinced that you should always ask permission: "better safe than sorry." I don't know if CC contributed to this culture of timidity. More likely, it was bullying copyright trolls who terrorized people into a reflex of asking permission for everything, always. As the creator of more than 30 books, hundreds of collages, and tens of thousands of essays and blog-posts, I am often on the receiving end of these permission requests. For example, people often ask me if they can use my CC licensed works in ways that the associated licenses clearly permit. I'm sure the people who email me for permission to do things I've already granted them permission to do think they're being polite, but I really wish they'd stop. When someone asks me if they can make a use permitted by my CC licenses, I need to carefully parse through their use to make sure they're not asking for something more. This is time-consuming work that often involves several volleys of email just to confirm that, no, they're just asking if they can do something I've already told them they can do. This is not a good use of anyone's time! By all means, drop me a note with a link to something you've remixed from my work. That's fun! It's a lot more fun than making me play detective in order to figure out if you're exceeding the license's permissions. There are also a lot of requests that clearly amount to fair use and/or di minimis usage. You don't need to email me to get my permission to read a brief passage from one of my books on your Youtube video! You don't need my permission to quote one of my stories in an English exam! What's more, the world would be a lot shittier if you did, so let's not act as though that's reasonable behavior, lest we shift the (already far too restrictive) norms, which might even lead to a legal change. Finally, there's the people who email me about their desire to make uses that are more (ahem) ambitious, but that no one could possibly find out about or get angry over…except for the fact that they emailed me to ask my permission. You want to make a tiny bootleg edition of one of my novels for your anarchist book fair? That's totally a copyright infringement, it's super-illegal, and if my publisher found out about it, I'm sure they'd send you a sphincter-puckering legal letter telling you to knock it off (and maybe even demanding that you disgorge the seven dollars, three bottlecaps and eleven cool feathers you took in trade for those pirate books). But my publisher won't ever find out about it – unless you email me asking for permission. I absolutely cannot give you permission to do this. I have a contract with my publisher promising that I will never authorize someone other than them to publish that book. Once you tell me about your intention to do this, I'm obliged to tell my publisher, so that they can tell you no in language that would strip paint off a barn. Buying a classroom set of books, but you also want to paste chunks of one of my books into your educational institution's classroom intranet for use as a teaching aid? There's no way my publisher would ever find out you did that, and if they did, sure, you'd also get a blood-curdling legal letter. But dude, all my books are DRM-free. You could have just pasted the text into your CMS. In what universe is my publisher going to pay one of their lawyers to review, adjudicate and paper over your request to make a use that you're not proposing to pay them for? Let's be clear: I'm not giving you permission to pirate my work. I already spend far too much of my time chasing down dickheads who sell competing editions of my books on Amazon and Audible. I'm sick to the back teeth of wrangling Ingram's takedown process to get rid of bootleg print editions of my books. What I'm saying is, all of your interactions with copyrighted works need not involve the author and publisher. There is a whole universe of uses that might technically violate copyright, might technically not fit into di minimis, first sale or fair use – but these are also uses that no one would ever find out. I get it. You may feel like you can't tell the difference between the kind of uses that no one would give a shit about; the uses that might attract a bone-chilling lawyer letter; and the uses that might land you in court. I'm sorry, but I can't help you figure that one out. I'm not a lawyer. Even if I was, I'm not your lawyer. This is one of those areas where I break with my friend, the wonderful John Hodgman. On his indispensable podcast "Judge John Hodgman," he frequently admonishes people who are uncertain if they're overstepping a bound in a commercial establishment to ask an employee for permission. For example: should you fill up a water glass with soda water from a self-serve dispenser? https://maximumfun.org/podcasts/judge-john-hodgman/ John says you should always ask the cashier. But I've worked jobs like that, and I can tell you that there were plenty of jobs where my boss felt very strongly that taking $0.0000001 worth of water and bubbles without paying for it was theft…and where I thought my boss was a dick for thinking that. If I pretended I didn't see you getting a glass of fizzy water, the worst that would happen is my boss would tell me to keep a closer eye on the customers lest they steal his precious CO2. But if you asked me whether you could fill your glass, and my boss caught me saying yes, I'd be fired. There's a lot of normal, perfectly fine stuff that technically violates copyright that I can't give you permission to do, because I've signed a contract with my publisher. If you ask me, I'll have to ask my editor, who will say no, even though he thinks it's fine, too. If I push it, he'll have to ask the lawyers, who will almost certainly also say no, even if they think it's fine, because it doesn't make sense to spend hours papering over a legal agreement with someone who wants to sell seven copies of a book at an anarchist book-fair or upload a couple chapters of a book to a school's intranet. Are there instances in which you might misjudge which category your use falls under and end up in court? I guess so. But if that's your concern, asking my permission does no good, because I'm just gonna tell you no. Life is hard. Read books. content_html_zh:
今天的链接

  • 最好请求原谅：除非绝对必要，否则不要按“不”家的门铃。
  • 嘿，看看这个：很高兴享受。
  • 客体持久性：RIP Poul Anderson； PC 论坛上的 P2P；女服务员将持卡用餐者偷来的身份证交给了她； PDX 禁止固定程序； 《数字经济法案》只是一个小问题；新西兰版权断线流程图；弗莱诉维迪科姆案关于天主教会；莫克西·马林斯派克个人资料； V&A 禁止素描；根斯巴克对第一部《惊奇故事》的介绍； “简单。”
  • 即将亮相：爱丁堡、悉尼、墨尔本、布莱顿、伦敦、南本德。
  • 最近出现：我去过的地方。
  • 最新书籍：你继续读它们，我会继续写它们。
  • 即将出版的书：就像我说的，我会继续写。
  • 版权页：剩下的都可以。


最好乞求原谅（永久链接）

从一开始，我就喜欢知识共享。 我和丽莎·雷因 (Lisa Rein)、马特·豪伊 (Matt Haughey) 和亚伦·斯沃茨 (Aaron Swartz) 一起编写了该网站的第一个版本，而我的第一部小说《魔法王国的落魄》是第一本在 CC 许可下发布的专业出版文本，就在 CC 本身推出几周后：

https://creativecommons.org/

在早期，CC 许可证主要是那些热衷于版权法、传说和诉讼的人感兴趣的。关于这些许可证的许多早期争论都变得深奥（但很重要！） 有关版权的问题；例如，CC 如何与版权的“限制和例外”互动。

你看，版权从来不意味着控制作品所有使用的绝对权利。 每个版权制度都包含一组“限制和例外”，供人们未经许可使用受版权保护的作品，即使版权所有者反对这种使用。 最著名的例子是“合理使用”，这是美国法律中的一个概念。

合理使用（可能）极其广泛，但它也极其“事实密集”——律师用这个词来描述那种答案几乎总是“视情况而定”的法律问题。 合理使用可能会让您复制整个作品，即使是出于商业目的。 它可能会让您根据现有作品创作新作品。 它可能会让你专门做这些事情来阻止人们购买原版。 但是……这要看情况。

如果您了解有关合理使用的任何信息，那么可能会了解用于确定使用是否公平的“四步测试”。 这四个步骤只是法官可能会向因侵犯版权而被起诉但声称自己正在合理使用的人提出的问题。 问题是：

我。 您使用的“性质和目的”是什么？ 你在做一些“变革性的事情”吗？ 你批评了这项工作吗？ 您是否将作品用于教育目的？

二. 您使用的工作性质是什么？ 它主要是事实性的（如新闻文章）还是创意性的（如短篇小说）？

三． 你承担了多少工作？ 你是否花费了超出你所需的时间来改变工作、完成你的批评、教导某人？

四． 您的使用对原版有什么影响？ 版权所有者是否因您的使用而遭受损失？

https://fairuse.stanford.edu/overview/fair-use/four-factors/

这些问题确实被写入美国版权法中，但是（无论好坏）你无法仅通过询问这些问题来判断使用是否“公平”。 合理使用最终要遵守“合理规则”，这是一项法律原则，意味着法律不应导致明显愚蠢的限制。 什么叫“明显愚蠢”？ 好吧，这就是棘手的部分——你必须说服法官！

例如，《风逝》一书的作者因采用《飘》的人物、情节和背景，从被奴役的非洲人的角度讲述同一个故事，而原著中的非洲人被剥夺了代理权和道德考虑，因此被起诉。 法院对《风已逝》作出的判决：

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Done_Gone

《风逝去》夺走了《乱世佳人》的“心”（III），但话又说回来，《逝去》具有高度变革性（I），《飘》也是一部虚构作品，有权获得最高级别的保护（II）。 更糟糕的是，《Done Gone》的目的是指出《Gone With》（I）的严重缺陷，从而直接损害原版（IV）的销售和许可。 任何声称可以通过检查四个因素（就好像它们是清单一样）来回答合理使用争议的人实际上并不理解合理使用：

https://pluralistic.net/2022/02/06/crypto-copyright-%f0%9f%a4%a1%f0%9f%92%a9/

但即使您已经了解了合理使用的事实密集型、细致入微的灵活性，您仍然不了解版权的限制和例外。 合理使用很重要，但还有“首次销售”原则，即购买某物后，您就拥有它，并且版权不能用来干扰您的传统财产权。 这就是为什么您可以买卖二手书、绘画、唱片和其他受版权保护的作品，即使它们出售时带有细则，表明您不得：

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirtsaeng_v._John_Wiley_%26_Sons,_Inc.

当谈到版权的限制和例外时，“合理使用”和“首次销售”是大问题，但同样重要的是小问题——真正的小问题。 与其他法律一样，版权受“di minimis”原则（来自较长的拉丁短语，翻译为“法律不关心琐事”）：

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_minimis

从技术上讲，踩到别人的院子可能会构成非法侵入。 但是，如果当你在他们家门前的人行道上行走时，你的鞋子擦到了他们的草坪，那就不是非法侵入。 或者，即使是非法侵入，也属于微量非法侵入，其程度太小，不会对法律造成影响。 许多潜在的版权侵犯行为（例如对书中的一段话拍照并将其发布到社交媒体）都很小，因此我们不需要对其进行合理使用分析。 它们都是小事，而“法律不关心小事”。

这些限制和例外均无需权利持有人许可即可适用。 即使它们让权利持有者愤怒，它们仍然适用。 它们是你的权利，作为公众的一员，作为作品的购买者，或者只是作为一个吹着你脑海中的歌曲的人的权利。

这就是早期深奥的知识共享版权争论的由来。 知识共享是一种正式编纂和传达使用版权作品许可的方式。 如果没有知识共享，向其他人提供使用您所创建的内容的合法可靠许可确实非常困难且昂贵。

如果我想让你把我的一个短篇小说改编成舞台剧，我们可能都应该以每小时几百美元的价格聘请版权律师来起草和审查一份合同，说明我的许可的真正含义。 更糟糕的是：即使我们付了律师费，我们也不太可能真正理解这笔交易的法律细节。 我们只需相信律师的话，合同中复杂的术语足以满足我们的目的。 在复杂性和费用之间，有很多潜在的创造性合作，如果掩盖起来会花费很多成本，所以即使它们会让每个参与者都高兴，它们也不值得去做。

知识共享通过其标准化许可证解决了这个问题，该许可证以简单的语言阐明了正在授予哪些权限。 更好的是，这些许可证是国际性的，被翻译成数十个国家的语言和法律。 这意味着您可以采用日本的 CC 许可短篇小说，使用意大利的 CC 许可 3D 模型为其制作动画，将其设置为印度尼西亚的 CC 许可配乐，然后在乌克兰发行，整个过程就可以了。

这些用途——将故事变成动画、使用 3D 模型、将配乐与视频同步——都是相当雄心勃勃的用途，特别是如果您要无限期地向公众提供最终结果。 掩盖这些用途是有意义的，知识共享使法律工作变得像在最终产品中链接到您的来源及其许可证一样简单。

但有很多用途不需要许可证——甚至是雄心勃勃的用途。 还记得风逝了吗？ 在某些情况下，您可以未经许可改编他人的故事，而是依赖版权的限制或例外。 当然，还有很多琐碎的用途，例如将照片粘贴到群聊中，这些用途都是微不足道的，也不需要许可。

这些版权灵活性至关重要。 想象一下，如果你只能批评某人的工作，如果他们允许你这样做！ 从 CC 成立之初，抄袭者就提出了严重的担忧，认为 CC 会教导人们，只有拥有许可证，才能重新混合他人的作品，无论是 CC 许可证还是与律师协商的许可证。

25 年后的今天！CC 取得了绝对的成功。 没有 CC，我们就不会有维基百科！ 您可以在 Youtube、Flickr、Bandcamp、Internet Archive 以及世界上许多最重要的学术和科学期刊上找到 CC 许可证。

而且，25 年后，全世界更加坚信您应该始终征求许可：“安全总比后悔好。” 我不知道CC是否助长了这种胆怯的文化。 更有可能的是，是欺凌版权巨魔，他们恐吓人们，让他们总是本能地要求获得一切许可。

作为 30 多本书、数百幅拼贴画以及数万篇论文和博客文章的创作者，我经常成为这些许可请求的接收端。

例如，人们经常问我是否可以按照相关许可证明确允许的方式使用我的 CC 许可作品。 我确信那些通过电子邮件向我请求允许做我已经允许他们做的事情的人认为他们很有礼貌，但我真的希望他们停止。 当有人问我他们是否可以使用我的 CC 许可证允许的用途时，我需要仔细分析他们的用途，以确保他们不会要求更多的东西。

这是一项耗时的工作，通常需要发送几封电子邮件来确认，不，他们只是询问是否可以做我已经告诉他们可以做的事情。 这对任何人的时间都没有很好的利用！ 无论如何，请给我留言，其中包含您从我的作品中重新混音的内容的链接。 真有趣！ 这比让我扮演侦探来查明你是否超出了许可证的权限有趣得多。

还有很多请求显然相当于合理使用和/或最低限度使用。 您无需给我发电子邮件来获得我的许可，即可在您的 Youtube 视频上阅读我的一本书中的简短段落！ 你不需要我的许可就可以在英语考试中引用我的故事！ 更重要的是，如果你这样做了，世界会变得更加糟糕，所以我们不要表现得好像这是合理的行为，以免我们改变（已经过于严格的）规范，这甚至可能导致法律变更。

最后，还有一些人给我发电子邮件，表达他们希望做出更（咳咳）雄心勃勃的用途，但没有人可能发现这一点或对此感到愤怒……除了他们给我发电子邮件征求我的许可这一事实。

你想为你的无政府主义书展制作我的一本小说的小盗版吗？ 这完全是侵犯版权，是超级非法的，如果我的出版商发现了这件事，我相信他们会给你发一封令人紧张的法律信函，告诉你停止这样做（甚至可能要求你交出你在盗版书交易中拿来的七美元、三个瓶盖和十一根很酷的羽毛）。

但我的出版商永远不会发现这件事——除非你给我发电子邮件请求许可。 我绝对不能允许你这样做。 我与出版商签订了一份合同，承诺我绝不会授权他们以外的任何人出版该书。 一旦你告诉我你打算这样做，我就有义务告诉我的出版商，这样他们就可以用会剥掉谷仓油漆的语言告诉你“不”。

购买一套课堂书籍，但您还想将我的其中一本书的大部分内容粘贴到您的教育机构的课堂内联网中作为教学辅助工具？ 我的出版商不可能发现你这么做了，如果他们发现了，当然，你也会收到一封令人毛骨悚然的法律信函。 但是老兄，我所有的书都是无 DRM 的。 您可以直接将文本粘贴到您的 CMS 中。 在什么情况下，我的出版商会付钱给他们的一位律师来审查、裁决和掩盖您的使用请求，而您不打算向他们支付费用？

让我们明确一点：我不会允许你盗版我的作品。 我已经花了太多的时间去追捕那些在亚马逊和 Audible 上销售我的书的竞争版本的白痴。 我厌倦了与英格拉姆处理我的书籍的盗版印刷版的删除过程的争论。

我的意思是，您与受版权保护的作品的所有互动都不需要涉及作者和出版商。 从技术上讲，有很多用途可能会侵犯版权，可能在技术上不符合最低限度、首次销售或合理使用的要求，但这些用途也是没有人会发现的。

我得到它。 您可能会觉得您无法区分无人关心的用途之间的区别；可能会引起令人不寒而栗的律师信的用途；以及可能会让您上法庭的用途。 抱歉，我无法帮助你解决这个问题。 我不是律师。 即使我是，我也不是你的律师。

这是我与我的朋友约翰·霍奇曼 (John Hodgman) 决裂的领域之一。 在他不可或缺的播客“Judge John Hodgman”中，他经常告诫那些不确定自己是否在商业机构中越界的人要征求员工的许可。 例如：您应该用自助饮水机将苏打水装满水杯吗？

https://maximumfun.org/podcasts/judge-john-hodgman/

约翰说你应该总是询问收银员。 但我也从事过这样的工作，我可以告诉你，在很多工作中，我的老板都强烈地认为，拿走价值 0.0000001 美元的水和泡沫而不付钱就是盗窃……而我认为我的老板这么想是个混蛋。 如果我假装没有看到你喝一杯碳酸水，最糟糕的情况就是我的老板会告诉我要密切关注顾客，以免他们偷走他宝贵的二氧化碳。 但如果你问我是否可以倒酒，而我的老板发现我说可以，我就会被解雇。

有很多正常的、完美的东西在技术上侵犯了版权，但我不能允许你这样做，因为我已经与我的出版商签订了合同。 如果你问我，我就得问我的编辑，他会说不，尽管他也认为这很好。 如果我坚持这样做，他将不得不询问律师，而律师几乎肯定也会拒绝，即使他们认为这很好，因为花几个小时与想要在无政府主义书展上出售七本一本书或将一本书的几章上传到学校内联网的人签订法律协议是没有意义的。

在某些情况下，您可能会误判您的使用属于哪一类别并最终上法庭？ 大概吧。 但如果你担心的是这个问题，那么征求我的许可是没有用的，因为我只会告诉你不。

生活很艰难。

读书。
